fields.title: Hosea
fields.subtitle: Hoshea, “Salvation”
fields.description: The prophet who preached through his own broken marriage, sent to the northern kingdom of Israel in its last prosperous, faithless decades before it fell to Assyria. Hosea marries Gomer, names their children No Compassion and Not My People, and buys back a wife who has left him, because God loves a people who have run after other gods. Between the judgments come some of the tenderest words in the Bible: the LORD leading his bride into the wilderness to speak tenderly to her, teaching Ephraim to walk, crying “How can I give you up?”, and asking for loyal love, not sacrifice. Set out line by line as the poetry it is, in the Open Word Bible, a new translation from the Hebrew given freely to the public domain, with an introduction to the book’s shape and meaning and a conclusion on where to read next.

qa.question: What is the book of Hosea?
qa.answer: The first of the twelve shorter prophetic books at the end of the Old Testament, often called the Minor Prophets because they are short, not because they matter less. Its fourteen chapters were spoken to the northern kingdom of Israel, which Hosea often calls Ephraim. Chapters 1–3 tell the story of the prophet’s marriage as a picture of God’s love for an unfaithful people; chapters 4–14 are poems that move between accusation and appeal, and the book ends with a call to return to the LORD and a promise that he will heal his people and love them freely (14:4).

qa.question: Who wrote the book of Hosea, and when?
qa.answer: The book presents itself as the word of the LORD that came to Hosea son of Beeri during the reigns of Jeroboam II of Israel and of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah of Judah (1:1). That puts his ministry roughly between 755 and 715 BC, the last decades of the northern kingdom before Samaria fell to Assyria in 722 BC. Most readers take Hosea himself to be the source of its oracles; many scholars think they were gathered and edited in Judah after the fall of the north, which would explain the lines addressed to Judah.

qa.question: Why did God tell Hosea to marry an unfaithful wife?
qa.answer: So that his marriage would preach. “Go, marry a promiscuous wife,” the LORD says, “for the land is wholly given to prostitution” (1:2): Hosea’s life with Gomer was to show Israel how its worship of Baal and other gods looked to the God who had made a covenant with it, and how he still loved it. Christians have understood the command in different ways. Some read it as literal, others think Gomer became unfaithful only after the marriage and the story is told from its end, and some interpreters, Jewish and Christian, have read it as a vision or acted parable. In chapter 3 Hosea buys back an adulterous wife, “just as the LORD loves the people of Israel”.

qa.question: What do the names of Hosea’s children mean?
qa.answer: Each is a message. Jezreel recalls the valley where King Jehu had seized the throne by slaughter, and announces judgment on his dynasty. Lo-ruhamah means “No Compassion” and Lo-ammi “Not My People”, the undoing of the covenant by which the LORD had made Israel his own. Then the names are reversed: “I will have compassion on No Compassion, and I will say to Not My People, ‘You are my people’” (2:23). Paul in Romans 9 and Peter in his first letter apply that reversal to Gentiles who come to belong to God.

qa.question: What does Hosea 6:6, “I want loyal love, not sacrifice”, mean?
qa.answer: That God wants faithfulness of heart and life more than religious ritual, “and knowledge of God more than burnt offerings”. The Hebrew word for loyal love, hesed, is the love that keeps covenant. Hosea did not reject sacrifice, but he said that worship without that love was worthless, like a ring worn by someone who has gone off with another. Jesus quoted the verse twice in Matthew’s Gospel, when he ate with sinners (9:13) and when his disciples were accused of breaking the Sabbath (12:7).

qa.question: Which translation of the Bible is this?
qa.answer: The Open Word Bible, a new translation made directly from the Hebrew and dedicated to the public domain, printed here at its Balanced level, which aims to be accurate and to read naturally aloud. The reasoning behind each of its sentences, with the Hebrew beside it, is published at openwordbible.org. The introduction and conclusion were written for this edition.

fields.title: Introduction
fields.body_html:
How can I give you up, Ephraim? How can I surrender you, Israel? How can I treat you like Admah? How can I make you like Zeboiim? Within me my heart turns over; all my compassion is stirred.

— Hosea 11:8

Hosea is the book in which God speaks like a betrayed husband and a heartbroken father. Other prophets thunder; Hosea grieves. He was sent to the northern kingdom of Israel in its last, feverish decades, and he told its people the hardest thing a prophet can say: that they did not know the God they worshipped. But he said it as no one had said it before, through the story of his own marriage.

The book is first of the twelve shorter prophets, the ones English readers call the Minor Prophets, meaning short rather than unimportant. It is also one of the most difficult books in the Bible. Its Hebrew is compressed and in places obscure, its poems change speaker without warning, and its images tumble over one another: a moth, a lion, a dove, a half-baked loaf, morning mist, a bear robbed of her cubs. Augustine, who wrote about it in The City of God, admitted that Hosea “speaks so very profoundly that it is laborious work to penetrate his meaning.”

Yet its heart is not hard to find at all. It beats in the verse above. Israel has earned the fate of the cities of the plain, and God cannot bring himself to give it up.

The last days of a kingdom

The book’s first verse sets Hosea in the reign of Jeroboam son of Joash over Israel, and of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah over Judah. That places the beginning of his work around the middle of the eighth century before Christ, and its end within a few years of the fall of the northern kingdom.

When Hosea began, Israel had never seemed stronger. Jeroboam II reigned for some forty years, pushed back his neighbours and brought wealth to the land. Amos, who preached in the same years, describes houses of ivory and couches of silk. Hosea saw the same prosperity and named what it had done: “When they had pasture, they ate their fill; they were full, and their hearts grew proud; that is why they forgot me.”

After Jeroboam died, the kingdom came apart. In the thirty years that followed, six kings sat on the throne of Samaria, and four of them were murdered by the men who replaced them. Hosea watched it happen: “All their kings have fallen, and not one of them calls on me.” Israel’s rulers lurched between paying tribute to Assyria and seeking help from Egypt, and Hosea has an image for that too: Ephraim “has become like a dove, easily fooled and without sense; they call to Egypt, they go to Assyria.” In 722 BC, after a siege of three years, Samaria fell to the Assyrians and its people were carried into exile. The book stands at the edge of that cliff.

Hosea is the northern kingdom’s own prophet. Amos came up from Judah to preach at Bethel; Hosea seems to have been one of the people he addressed, and he speaks of its towns, its shrines and its history from the inside. He often calls the nation Ephraim, after its largest tribe, and the name comes back almost forty times.

A marriage that preached

The book begins with a command that has troubled readers ever since:

When the LORD first spoke through Hosea, the LORD said to him, “Go, marry a promiscuous wife and have children born of promiscuity, for the land is wholly given to prostitution; it has turned away from following the LORD.”

— Hosea 1:2

Hosea marries Gomer daughter of Diblaim, and she bears three children, each named by God as a sermon. The first is Jezreel, the valley where King Jehu had seized the throne in a bloodbath nearly a century earlier; the dynasty that began there would now be brought to account. The second is a daughter named No Compassion, “for I will no longer show compassion to the house of Israel.” The third is a son named Not My People, “because you are not my people, and I will not be yours.” The last name undoes the covenant itself, the bond by which the LORD had made Israel his people and himself their God.

Then, before the first chapter is over, the sentence is reversed. The people will be as countless as the sand, and “In the very place where they were told, ‘You are not my people,’ they will be told, ‘You are children of the living God.’” The pattern of the whole book is there in miniature: judgment spoken in full, and then a love that refuses to let judgment have the last word.

Chapter 2 turns the marriage into a courtroom poem. The wife has run after lovers, believing that they gave her grain and wine and oil, when “it was I who gave her the grain, the new wine, and the olive oil.” In Hosea’s day Baal was worshipped as the storm god who sent the rain and made the fields fruitful, and Israel had come to give him the thanks that belonged to the LORD. So the LORD will take back his gifts until she remembers who gave them. And then, astonishingly, the punishment becomes a courtship:

Therefore I am going to woo her; I will lead her into the wilderness and speak tenderly to her. There I will give her back her vineyards and make the valley of Achor a door of hope. There she will respond as in the days of her youth, as on the day she came up from the land of Egypt.

— Hosea 2:14–15

The valley of Achor, “trouble”, was where Achan was stoned when Israel first entered the land. The place of the first disaster will become the door. And in the wilderness, where the LORD first took Israel as his own, he will betroth her again:

I will betroth you to me forever. I will betroth you to me with righteousness and justice, with loyal love and compassion. I will betroth you to me with faithfulness, and you will know the LORD.

— Hosea 2:19–20

Notice the dowry. The bridegroom pays it, and what he pays is himself: righteousness, justice, loyal love, compassion and faithfulness. The chapter ends by renaming the children. No Compassion will be shown compassion; to Not My People God will say “You are my people,” and he will say “You are my God.”

In chapter 3 Hosea is told to “Go again, love a woman who is loved by another man and is an adulteress, just as the LORD loves the people of Israel.” He buys her back, for silver and barley, and she must wait with him many days, as Israel will wait without king or sacrifice before it turns back to “the LORD their God and David their king.”

Readers have long asked what really happened. Some take the story at its plainest: God told the prophet to marry a woman known to be unfaithful. Others think Gomer was faithful when Hosea married her and only later went astray, and that chapter 1 tells the story with its end already in view. Some interpreters, Jewish and Christian, have read the marriage as a vision or an acted parable rather than a literal command. Most readers think the woman of chapter 3 is Gomer herself, taken back; a few think she is another woman. The book does not settle these questions. What it makes unmistakable is that the prophet’s pain is meant to let us feel God’s. Israel had broken God’s heart, and Hosea knew what that meant from the inside.

“No knowledge of God in the land”

From chapter 4 to the end the book is a long series of poems, hard to divide neatly, that move back and forth between accusation and appeal. It opens like a court case: “the LORD has a charge to bring against those who live in the land: there is no faithfulness, no loyal love, and no knowledge of God in the land.”

Those three missing things are Hosea’s great words. Faithfulness is being true to one’s word. Loyal love, the Hebrew hesed, is the love that keeps covenant when keeping it costs something. And knowledge of God, for Hosea, is not information about him but intimacy with him, the knowing of a husband and wife. Its absence explains everything else: “Cursing, lying, murder, stealing and adultery!”

Hosea lays much of the blame at the feet of the priests, who should have taught the people and instead fed on their sins: “My people are perishing for lack of knowledge.” And so it will be “like people, like priest.” Worship had gone wild on every hilltop. People consulted pieces of wood; the shrines at Bethel and Gilgal were full of sacrifice and empty of God. Hosea’s scorn for the golden calf set up at Bethel is withering: “a craftsman made it; it is not God.” He even renames Bethel, “house of God”, as Beth-aven, “house of wickedness”.

Politics fares no better. “They set up kings, but not by me.” Israel sought safety in treaties, in fortified towns, in horses, in anyone but God. Hosea’s images for this drift are some of the sharpest in Scripture: “Ephraim is a flat loaf left unturned”, burnt on one side and raw on the other; strangers have eaten up his strength, and “gray hairs are scattered on his head, but he does not know it.” And over it all stands a proverb that has passed into common speech: “They sow the wind, and they will reap the whirlwind.”

Loyal love, not sacrifice

At the centre of the book stands a moment of apparent repentance. The people say to one another:

“Come, let us return to the LORD. It is he who has torn us, and he will heal us; he has struck us down, and he will bandage our wounds. After two days he will bring us back to life; on the third day he will raise us up, so that we may live in his presence. Let us know the LORD; let us press on to know him. His coming is as certain as the sunrise; he will come to us like the showers, like the spring rain that waters the land.”

— Hosea 6:1–3

It sounds beautiful, and it is. But God’s answer shows that it is not enough. The people expect God to come back as surely as the sunrise; God replies that their love comes and goes like the dew:

What am I to do with you, Ephraim? What am I to do with you, Judah? Your loyal love is like the morning mist, like the dew that vanishes early in the day. That is why I have cut them down by the prophets; I have killed them with the words of my mouth, and the judgment on you goes out like the light. For I want loyal love, not sacrifice, and knowledge of God more than burnt offerings.

— Hosea 6:4–6

The last verse is one Jesus loved. Twice in Matthew’s Gospel he quotes it to critics who cared more for ritual than for people: when he ate with tax collectors and sinners, “Go and learn what this saying means: ‘I want mercy, not sacrifice’”, and when his disciples picked grain on the Sabbath. Hosea did not mean that sacrifice was worthless. He meant that ritual without loyalty is like a wedding ring worn by someone who has gone off with another.

The promise of being raised up “on the third day” was read by many early Christian writers as a hint of the resurrection. Hosea himself was speaking of the nation’s recovery, and readers differ on how far to press the words; but the shape of Israel’s hope, death and then life from God, is the shape of the gospel.

“How can I give you up?”

Chapter 11 is the summit of the book, and one of the tenderest passages in the Old Testament. Here the picture changes from husband to father:

When Israel was a boy, I loved him, and out of Egypt I called my son.

— Hosea 11:1

God remembers Israel’s childhood the way a parent does: “it was I who taught Ephraim to walk, holding them by the arms”, leading them “with ropes of love”, bending down to feed them. And the more he called, the further they ran. Justice would leave them to the fate of Admah and Zeboiim, towns destroyed with Sodom and Gomorrah. Then comes the verse at the head of this introduction, and the reason God gives for mercy:

I will not act on my burning anger; I will not turn to destroy Ephraim again. For I am God and not a human, the Holy One among you, and I will not come in fury.

— Hosea 11:9

We might have expected the opposite. A human being, wronged like this, would take revenge; it is because God is holy, not in spite of it, that he will not come in fury. His holiness is not only his purity but his otherness, and part of what makes him other is a love that outlasts betrayal.

Matthew’s Gospel hears in “out of Egypt I called my son” a pattern fulfilled when the child Jesus is brought back from Egypt. The Son who is called out of Egypt this time is the one who will be faithful where Israel was not.

Jacob, the wilderness, and death

The last chapters reach back into Israel’s past to explain its present. Chapter 12 recalls Jacob, the nation’s ancestor: “In the womb he grabbed his brother by the heel, and in his full strength he contended with God.” Yet at the Jabbok “he wept and begged for his favor.” His children have inherited his grasping without his tears. Chapter 13 recalls the wilderness, where God cared for them “in a land of burning drought”, and how they forgot him the moment they were full. There is a stern claim at its centre: “there is no savior except me.”

The judgments grow darker: the lion, the leopard, the bear robbed of her cubs. And then a verse of strange double edge:

Shall I ransom them from the power of Sheol? Shall I redeem them from death? O death, where are your plagues? O Sheol, where is your sting? Compassion is hidden from my eyes.

— Hosea 13:14

In its setting it may be a summons to death to do its worst, and many translations, this one among them, read the first lines as questions. But the apostle Paul heard in it something more. Writing of the resurrection, he takes up its words and turns them into a taunt over a defeated enemy: “Death, where is your victory? Death, where is your sting?”

Return

Hosea’s last chapter is a call to come home, with the very words to say:

Return, Israel, to the LORD your God, for your guilt has made you stumble. Take words with you and return to the LORD. Say to him, “Take away all guilt, and accept what is good, and we will offer our lips in place of bulls.

— Hosea 14:1–2

The prayer God gives them renounces every false hope Hosea has named: “Assyria cannot save us; we will not ride on horses. Never again will we say ‘Our god’ to what our own hands have made, for in you the orphan finds compassion.” And God answers it before it is finished:

I will heal their unfaithfulness; I will love them freely, for my anger has turned away from them. To Israel I will be like the dew; he will blossom like a lily and send down his roots like the cedars of Lebanon.

— Hosea 14:4–5

The dew that once stood for Israel’s fickle love now stands for God’s faithful one. The nation that was a withered root will blossom like a lily and grow like the cedars of Lebanon. And the book that began with a broken marriage ends with God saying, “your fruit comes from me.”

Hosea in the New Testament

Beyond the sayings already mentioned, the apostles found in Hosea one of their clearest pictures of the gospel going out to the nations. Paul, in Romans 9, and Peter, in his first letter, take up the renaming of Hosea’s children, “Not My People” becoming “My People”, and apply it to Gentiles who had never belonged to God and now do: “At one time you were no people at all; now you are God’s people.” Jesus, on the way to the cross, quotes the cry of 10:8, people calling on the mountains to cover them and the hills to fall on them, and the book of Revelation echoes it. Through the long story of Christian reading, Hosea’s marriage has been heard as the story of Christ and his church: a bridegroom who goes after an unfaithful bride and pays the price to bring her home.

How to read Hosea

Read the first three chapters slowly, as one piece, since everything else depends on them. Then read chapters 4–14 in larger stretches rather than verse by verse. The poems are short and change direction quickly, and their power is cumulative, like listening to someone pour out a grief that keeps breaking into hope. Chapters 6, 11 and 14 are the places to pause.

Expect to be puzzled now and then. Hosea refers to places and events his first hearers knew well: Gibeah, where a terrible crime once led to civil war; Baal-peor, where Israel first worshipped the gods of Moab; Gilgal and Bethel, the great shrines of his own day. When a line is obscure, read on; the main thread is never lost for long.

Listen for the two great pictures, the husband and the father, and for the words that keep returning: return, know, loyal love, Egypt, Assyria, prostitution and healing. Above all, listen for the voice of God, which in Hosea is passionate, wounded and stubbornly kind. The book is less a set of arguments than a love letter written in tears.

About this translation

The text in this edition is the Open Word Bible, a new translation made directly from the Hebrew and given freely to the public domain. It is printed here at its Balanced level, which aims to be accurate and to read naturally aloud. A few of its choices in Hosea are worth knowing before you begin.

Poetry. Almost all of Hosea is poetry, and this edition prints each line on its own, as the Hebrew sets it out. The narrative of chapters 1 and 3 is printed as prose.

“The LORD.” Where the Hebrew uses God’s personal name, the four letters often written Yahweh, this translation follows long Jewish and Christian custom and writes “the LORD”. In 12:5 the name is joined to a title that older Bibles render “hosts”: “The LORD is the God of Armies”.

“Loyal love.” The Hebrew hesed, which older Bibles call “mercy”, “goodness” or “lovingkindness”, is translated “loyal love” throughout, so that Hosea’s key word can be heard each time it comes: “For I want loyal love, not sacrifice.”

The children’s names. The names of Gomer’s second and third children, often left in Hebrew as Lo-ruhamah and Lo-ammi, are translated, “No Compassion” and “Not My People”, so that every reader hears what Hosea’s hearers heard. In 2:16 the same is done with a play on words: “you will call me ‘My husband’; you will no longer call me ‘My Baal’”, since baal was also an ordinary word for a husband or master.

Numbering. The Hebrew divides Hosea’s chapters a little differently from English Bibles, in chapters 1–2 and 11–14. This edition follows the English chapters, and the references in it follow the English numbering.

For the reasoning behind every sentence of the translation, with the Hebrew beside it, see the Open Word Bible itself at openwordbible.org.

fields.title: Hosea 1
fields.body_html:
The word of the LORD to Hosea

1The LORD’s word came to Hosea son of Beeri during the reigns of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah over Judah, and during the reign of Jeroboam son of Joash over Israel. 2When the LORD first spoke through Hosea, the LORD said to him, “Go, marry a promiscuous wife and have children born of promiscuity, for the land is wholly given to prostitution; it has turned away from following the LORD.” 3So Hosea went and married Gomer daughter of Diblaim, and she became pregnant and bore him a son. 4Then the LORD said to him, “Name him Jezreel, for in a little while I will punish the house of Jehu for the blood shed at Jezreel, and I will bring the kingdom of the house of Israel to an end. 5On that day I will break Israel’s bow in the valley of Jezreel.” 6Gomer became pregnant again and gave birth to a daughter. Then the LORD said to Hosea, “Name her No Compassion, for I will no longer show compassion to the house of Israel or forgive them in any way. 7But I will show compassion to the house of Judah, and I will save them by the LORD their God. I will not save them by bow or sword or battle, or by horses and horsemen.” 8After Gomer had weaned No Compassion, she became pregnant and gave birth to a son. 9Then the LORD said, “Name him Not My People, because you are not my people, and I will not be yours.”

10Yet the number of the people of Israel will be like the sand of the sea, which no one can measure or count. In the very place where they were told, “You are not my people,” they will be told, “You are children of the living God.” 11The people of Judah and the people of Israel will be gathered together. They will appoint one leader for themselves and will go up out of the land, for the day of Jezreel will be great.
fields.summary: God tells Hosea to marry Gomer, an unfaithful wife, as a picture of Israel’s unfaithfulness, and their children are given names of judgment.

fields.title: Hosea 2
fields.body_html:
Children of the living God

1Say to your brothers, “My People,”
and to your sisters, “Shown Compassion.”
2Bring a charge against your mother, bring a charge,
because she is not my wife, and I am not her husband.
She must put away her prostitution from her face
and her adultery from between her breasts,
3or I will strip her naked
and leave her as bare as on the day she was born.
I will make her like a wilderness, turn her into a parched land,
and let her die of thirst.
4I will not show compassion to her children,
because they are children born of promiscuity.
5Their mother has prostituted herself;
she who conceived them has behaved shamefully.
For she said, “I will follow my lovers, who give me my food and water,
my wool and flax,
my oil and drink.”
6Therefore I will block your way with thorns,
and I will wall her in,
so that she cannot find her paths.
7She will chase after her lovers but not catch them;
she will look for them but not find them.
Then she will say, “I will go back to my first husband,
for I was better off then than now.”
8She did not acknowledge
that it was I who gave her the grain, the new wine, and the olive oil,
and who lavished on her the silver and gold that they used for Baal.
9So I will take back my grain at harvest time
and my new wine in its season.
I will snatch away my wool and my flax,
which were to cover her nakedness.
10Now I will lay bare her lewdness before her lovers’ eyes,
and no one will rescue her from my hand.
11I will put an end to all her celebrations,
her festivals, her new moons, and her Sabbaths,
and all her appointed feasts.
12I will lay waste her vines and her fig trees,
of which she said, “These are my pay, which my lovers gave me.”
I will turn them into a thicket,
and the wild animals will eat them up.
13I will punish her for the feast days of the Baals, when she burned offerings to them,
put on her rings and her jewelry,
and went after her lovers,
but forgot me, declares the LORD.

Led back into the wilderness

14Therefore I am going to woo her;
I will lead her into the wilderness
and speak tenderly to her.
15There I will give her back her vineyards
and make the valley of Achor a door of hope.
There she will respond as in the days of her youth,
as on the day she came up from the land of Egypt.

16On that day, declares the LORD, you will call me “My husband”;
you will no longer call me “My Baal.”
17I will remove the names of the Baals from her mouth,
and they will no longer be invoked by name.
18On that day I will make a covenant on their behalf
with the wild animals and the birds of the sky
and the creatures that move along the ground.
I will break bow and sword and battle and remove them from the land,
and I will let them lie down in safety.
19I will betroth you to me forever.
I will betroth you to me with righteousness and justice,
with loyal love and compassion.
20I will betroth you to me with faithfulness,
and you will know the LORD.

21On that day I will answer, declares the LORD.
I will answer the heavens,
and they will answer the earth.
22The earth will answer the grain, the new wine, and the olive oil,
and they will answer Jezreel.
23I will sow her for myself in the land.
I will have compassion on No Compassion,
and I will say to Not My People, “You are my people,”
and he will say, “You are my God.”
fields.summary: Israel will one day again be called children of the living God. Israel is like an unfaithful wife who chased her lovers, and God will strip her bare, yet God will lead her into the wilderness, speak tenderly to her and betroth her forever in faithfulness.

fields.title: Hosea 3
fields.body_html:
Go again and love

1The LORD said to me, “Go again, love a woman who is loved by another man and is an adulteress, just as the LORD loves the people of Israel, though they turn to other gods and love raisin cakes.” 2So I bought her for myself for about 6 ounces of silver and about 9 bushels of barley. 3Then I said to her, “You must stay with me for many days. You must not prostitute yourself or belong to any man, and I will do the same toward you.” 4For the people of Israel will live for many days with no king or prince, no sacrifice or sacred pillar, no ephod or household gods. 5Afterward the people of Israel will turn back and seek the LORD their God and David their king. In days to come they will come trembling to the LORD and to his goodness.
fields.summary: God tells Hosea to love his wife again, as God loves Israel, and Israel will return to God in the last days.

fields.title: Hosea 4
fields.body_html:
The LORD’s case against Israel

1Hear the word of the LORD, people of Israel,
for the LORD has a charge to bring against those who live in the land:
there is no faithfulness, no loyal love, and no knowledge of God in the land.
2Cursing, lying, murder, stealing and adultery!
They break through every limit, and one killing follows another.
3So the land mourns, and all who live in it waste away, along with the wild animals and the birds of the sky;
even the fish of the sea are swept away.
4Yet let no one bring a charge, and let no one accuse another,
for your people are like those who contend with a priest.
5By day you will stumble,
and by night the prophet will stumble with you,
and I will destroy your mother.
6My people are perishing for lack of knowledge.
Since you have rejected knowledge, I reject you as my priest;
since you have forgotten the instruction of your God,
I too will forget your children.
7The more they increased, the more they sinned against me;
I will turn their glory into shame.
8They feed on the sin of my people
and set their appetite on their guilt.
9So it will be: like people, like priest.
I will punish them for their ways
and repay them for their deeds.
10They will eat but not be satisfied;
they will prostitute themselves but not increase,
because they have stopped heeding the LORD.
11Prostitution, wine and new wine take away understanding.
12My people consult a piece of wood,
and their stick gives them answers.
A spirit of prostitution has led them astray,
and they have prostituted themselves, leaving their God.
13They offer sacrifices on the tops of the mountains and burn offerings on the hills,
under oak, poplar and terebinth, since their shade is good.
That is why your daughters prostitute themselves
and your daughters-in-law commit adultery.
14I will not punish your daughters for prostituting themselves, nor your daughters-in-law for committing adultery,
since the men themselves slip away with prostitutes
and sacrifice alongside shrine prostitutes.
A people without understanding will come to ruin.
15Though you, Israel, prostitute yourself,
do not let Judah become guilty.
Stay away from Gilgal; do not go up to Beth-aven;
and do not take the oath, “As surely as the LORD lives.”
16Israel is stubborn, like a stubborn heifer.
Can the LORD now pasture them like a lamb in an open meadow?
17Ephraim is joined to idols; let him alone.
18When their drinking is over,
they prostitute themselves again and again;
her rulers dearly love what is shameful.
19A wind has bundled her up in its wings,
and they will be put to shame because of their sacrifices.
fields.summary: God brings a charge against Israel: there is no faithfulness, no loyal love and no knowledge of God in the land, and the priests have failed.

fields.title: Hosea 5
fields.body_html:
A snare at Mizpah

1Hear this, you priests! Pay attention, house of Israel! Listen, royal house!
The judgment is against you,
for you have been a trap at Mizpah,
a net spread out on Tabor.
2The rebels have sunk deep in slaughter,
but I will discipline them all.
3I know Ephraim;
Israel is not hidden from me.
For now, Ephraim, you have prostituted yourself;
Israel has become unclean.
4Their deeds will not let them return to their God,
because a spirit of prostitution is in them,
and they do not know the LORD.
5Israel’s pride testifies against him;
Israel and Ephraim will stumble in their guilt,
and Judah will stumble with them.
6With their flocks and their herds they will go to seek the LORD, but they will not find him;
he has withdrawn from them.
7They have betrayed the LORD;
the children they have borne are illegitimate.
Now the new moon will consume them with their fields.

Sound the alarm in Gibeah

8Blow the ram’s horn in Gibeah,
the trumpet in Ramah!
Sound the battle cry at Beth-aven:
“Behind you, Benjamin!”
9Ephraim will be laid waste on the day of punishment;
among the tribes of Israel I declare what will surely come.
10The leaders of Judah have become like those who move boundary stones;
I will pour out my wrath on them like water.
11Ephraim is oppressed, crushed under judgment,
because he was determined to follow mere commands.
12I am like a moth to Ephraim,
like rot to the house of Judah.
13When Ephraim saw his sickness and Judah his wound,
Ephraim went to Assyria
and sent to the great king.
But he cannot heal you,
and your wound will not go away.
14For I will be like a lion to Ephraim,
like a young lion to the house of Judah.
I, yes I, will tear them to pieces and go away;
I will carry them off, and no one will rescue them.
15I will return to my place
until they confess their guilt and seek my face.
In their distress they will search for me eagerly.
fields.summary: Judgment is coming on Israel and Judah for their idolatry, and God will withdraw until they seek God.

fields.title: Hosea 6
fields.body_html:
Come, let us return

1“Come, let us return to the LORD.
It is he who has torn us, and he will heal us;
he has struck us down, and he will bandage our wounds.
2After two days he will bring us back to life;
on the third day he will raise us up,
so that we may live in his presence.
3Let us know the LORD; let us press on to know him.
His coming is as certain as the sunrise;
he will come to us like the showers,
like the spring rain that waters the land.”
4What am I to do with you, Ephraim?
What am I to do with you, Judah?
Your loyal love is like the morning mist,
like the dew that vanishes early in the day.
5That is why I have cut them down by the prophets;
I have killed them with the words of my mouth,
and the judgment on you goes out like the light.
6For I want loyal love, not sacrifice,
and knowledge of God more than burnt offerings.
7But like Adam they have broken the covenant;
there they have betrayed me.
8Gilead is a city of evildoers,
marked with bloody footprints.
9Like bandits lying in wait for a victim, so is a gang of priests;
they murder on the road to Shechem;
what they have done is a vile crime.
10In the house of Israel I have seen something horrible:
Ephraim’s prostitution is there, and Israel has become unclean.
11Judah, a harvest is set for you too.
Whenever I would restore the fortunes of my people,
fields.summary: The people say, “Let us return to God,” but their loyalty is like morning mist, and God desires loyal love more than sacrifice.

fields.title: Hosea 7
fields.body_html:
When I would heal Israel

1whenever I would heal Israel, Ephraim’s guilt comes to light, and the wicked deeds of Samaria,
for they deal in lies.
Thieves break into houses;
gangs of raiders rob in the streets.
2They never stop to think
that I remember all their wickedness.
Now their deeds hem them in;
they are always in my sight.
3They delight the king with their wickedness,
and the officials with their lies.
4They are all adulterers;
they are like an oven heated by the baker,
who stops stirring up the fire
from the time he kneads the dough until it has risen.
5On our king’s festival day
the officials made him sick with the heat of wine,
and he joined hands with mockers.
6For their hearts are like an oven as they draw near with their schemes;
all night long their baker sleeps;
in the morning the oven blazes like a flaming fire.
7They are all as hot as an oven,
and they consume their rulers.
All their kings have fallen,
and not one of them calls on me.
8Ephraim mixes himself with the nations;
Ephraim is a flat loaf left unturned.
9Foreigners have eaten up his strength,
but he does not know it;
gray hairs are scattered on his head,
but he does not know it.
10Israel’s pride testifies against him,
yet they have not returned to the LORD their God
or sought him in spite of all this.
11Ephraim has become like a dove,
easily fooled and without sense;
they call to Egypt, they go to Assyria.
12When they go, I will throw my net over them;
I will bring them down like birds from the sky;
I will discipline them
as their assembly has been told.

Woe to them

13Woe to them, for they have strayed from me!
Ruin to them, for they have rebelled against me!
I would redeem them,
but they tell lies about me.
14They do not cry out to me from the heart
when they wail on their beds.
They gather together for grain and new wine, and turn away from me.
15I trained them and strengthened their arms,
yet they plot evil against me.
16They turn, but not to the One above; they are like a bow that will not shoot true.
Their officials will fall by the sword because of their insolent tongues.
For this they will be laughed at in the land of Egypt.
fields.summary: Israel is like a silly dove, turning to Egypt and Assyria instead of God.

fields.title: Hosea 8
fields.body_html:
Sound the alarm

1Put the ram’s horn to your lips!
An enemy swoops like an eagle over the house of the LORD,
because they have broken my covenant
and rebelled against my instruction.
2They cry out to me,
“My God, we, Israel, know you!”
3Israel has rejected what is good;
an enemy will chase him down.
4They set up kings, but not by me;
they appointed officials without my approval.
With their silver and gold they made themselves idols,
to their own destruction.
5Your calf is rejected, Samaria!
My anger burns against them.
How long will they be unable to become clean?
6This thing too comes from Israel:
a craftsman made it;
it is not God.
The calf of Samaria will be smashed to splinters.
7They sow the wind, and they will reap the whirlwind.
The standing grain has no head; it will make no flour.
Even if it did,
foreigners would swallow it up.
8Israel has been swallowed up;
now they are among the nations
like a jar that no one wants.
9They have gone up to Assyria,
like a wild donkey roaming on its own.
Ephraim has paid for lovers.
10Even though they hire lovers among the nations, I will now gather them together,
and soon they will begin to suffer
under the burden of the king of princes.
11Ephraim has built many altars for sin,
but they have become altars for sinning.
12Though I write down for him
the many things of my instruction,
they are treated as something foreign.
13They offer sacrifices as gifts to me and eat the meat,
but the LORD does not accept them.
Now he will remember their guilt and punish their sins;
they will go back to Egypt.
14Israel has forgotten his Maker and built palaces,
and Judah has built many fortified towns.
But I will send fire on his towns,
and it will burn up their fortresses.
fields.summary: Israel has rejected what is good and made idols, sowing the wind and reaping the whirlwind.

fields.title: Hosea 9
fields.body_html:
No joy at the harvest

1Do not rejoice, Israel; do not exult like the other nations,
for you have prostituted yourself and left your God.
You have loved a prostitute’s pay
on every threshing floor heaped with grain.
2Neither threshing floor nor winepress will feed them,
and the new wine will let her down.
3They will not stay in the land of the LORD.
Ephraim will go back to Egypt,
and in Assyria they will eat unclean food.
4They will pour out no wine offerings to the LORD, and their sacrifices will give him no pleasure.
They will be like mourners’ bread to them;
all who eat it will become unclean.
Their bread will be for their own hunger;
it will not come into the house of the LORD.
5What will you do on the day of the appointed festival,
on the day of the feast of the LORD?
6For look, even if they escape the destruction,
Egypt will gather them in, and Memphis will bury them.
Nettles will take over their treasures of silver,
and thorns will grow in their tents.
7The days of punishment have come; the days of repayment have come.
Let Israel know it!
“The prophet is a fool; the man of the Spirit is mad!” you say,
because your guilt is so great
and your hostility so deep.
8The prophet is the watchman over Ephraim, with my God;
yet a fowler’s snare lies on all his paths,
and hostility waits for him in the house of his God.
9They have sunk deep into corruption, as at Gibeah in days gone by.
He will remember their guilt;
he will punish their sins.

Grapes in the wilderness

10Like grapes in the desert, I found Israel;
like the first ripe fruit on the fig tree in its first season,
I saw your ancestors.
But they came to the Baal of Peor and dedicated themselves to the Shameful One,
and they became as detestable as the thing they loved.
11As for Ephraim, their glory will fly away like a bird:
no birth, no pregnancy, no conception.
12Even if they raise children,
I will take them until no one is left.
Yes, woe to them when I turn away from them!
13Ephraim, as I have seen, was like Tyre, set in a pleasant meadow;
but Ephraim will lead out his children to the killer.
14Give them, LORD — what should you give them?
Give them wombs that miscarry
and breasts that are dry.
15All their evil is in Gilgal; there I came to hate them.
Because of their evil deeds
I will drive them from my house.
I will love them no more;
all their officials are rebels.
16Ephraim is struck down;
their root has dried up, and they will bear no fruit.
Even if they give birth,
I will put to death the dear children of their womb.

17My God will reject them
because they have not listened to him,
and they will wander among the nations.
fields.summary: Israel will not stay in the land but return to Egypt and eat unclean food in Assyria.

fields.title: Hosea 10
fields.body_html:
A spreading vine

1Israel was a spreading vine
that yielded fruit for itself.
The more his fruit increased, the more altars he built;
the better his land became,
the finer the sacred pillars they made.
2Their heart is false; now they must bear their guilt.
He himself will break down their altars
and destroy their sacred pillars.
3Now they will say,
“We have no king,
because we did not fear the LORD.
And a king — what could he do for us?”
4They speak empty words,
swearing false oaths and making agreements.
So justice springs up like poisonous weeds
in the furrows of a field.
5The people of Samaria will be afraid
for the calf of Beth-aven.
Its people will mourn over it, and its idol-priests will wail over it
and over its glory, because it has gone from them into exile.
6The idol itself will be carried to Assyria
as tribute for the great king.
Ephraim will be put to shame,
and Israel will be ashamed of its own plans.
7As for Samaria, her king will be cut off
like a twig on the surface of the water.
8The high places of Aven, the sin of Israel, will be destroyed;
thorn and thistle will spring up over their altars.
Then they will cry to the mountains, “Cover us!”
and they will cry to the hills, “Fall on us!”

Since the days of Gibeah

9Since the days of Gibeah you have sinned, Israel;
there they have remained.
Will not war overtake them in Gibeah,
war against the wrongdoers?
10When I please, I will discipline them;
nations will be gathered against them
when they are harnessed for their double guilt.
11Ephraim was a trained heifer that loved to thresh,
but I put a yoke on her fine neck.
I will harness Ephraim; Judah must plow;
Jacob must break up the ground for himself.
12Sow righteousness for yourselves; reap a harvest of loyal love;
plow up your unplowed ground.
It is time to seek the LORD,
until he comes and rains righteousness on you.
13You have plowed wickedness and harvested injustice; you have eaten the fruit of deceit,
because you trusted in your own way and in your many warriors.
14The roar of war will rise among your people,
and every one of your fortresses will be laid waste,
just as Shalman laid waste Beth-arbel on the day of battle,
when mothers were dashed in pieces together with their children.
15This is what Bethel will bring on you,
because your wickedness is so great.
At dawn the king of Israel will be completely cut off.
fields.summary: Israel is a luxuriant vine that multiplied its altars, and its calf idol and its king will be carried away.

fields.title: Hosea 11
fields.body_html:
Out of Egypt I called my son

1When Israel was a boy, I loved him,
and out of Egypt I called my son.
2The more they called to them,
the more they went away from them.
They sacrificed to the Baals
and burned offerings to carved idols.
3Yet it was I who taught Ephraim to walk,
holding them by the arms,
but they did not know that I was the one who healed them.
4I led them with human cords, with ropes of love.
To them I was like someone who lifts the yoke off their jaws,
and I bent down to them and fed them.
5He will not go back to the land of Egypt;
Assyria will be his king instead,
because they refused to return to me.
6A sword will sweep through their cities;
it will break the bars of their gates and consume them,
because of their own schemes.
7My people are set on turning away from me.
Though they are called to the One on high,
not one of them rises up.
8How can I give you up, Ephraim? How can I surrender you, Israel?
How can I treat you like Admah?
How can I make you like Zeboiim?
Within me my heart turns over;
all my compassion is stirred.
9I will not act on my burning anger;
I will not turn to destroy Ephraim again.
For I am God and not a human,
the Holy One among you,
and I will not come in fury.
10They will follow the LORD, who will roar like a lion.
When he roars,
children will come trembling from the west.
11They will come trembling like birds from Egypt,
like doves from the land of Assyria,
and I will settle them in their homes, declares the LORD.

12Ephraim has surrounded me with lies,
the house of Israel with deceit,
and Judah still runs wild against God,
against the faithful Holy One.
fields.summary: When Israel was a child, God loved him and called him out of Egypt, taught him to walk and led him with ropes of love. God’s compassion will not let Israel be destroyed.

fields.title: Hosea 12
fields.body_html:
Surrounded with lies

1Ephraim tends the wind like a flock and chases the east wind;
all day long he piles up lies and violence.
They make a treaty with Assyria
and send olive oil to Egypt.
2The LORD has a case to bring against Judah;
he will punish Jacob for his ways
and repay him for what he has done.
3In the womb he grabbed his brother by the heel,
and in his full strength he contended with God.
4He contended with the angel and came through victorious;
he wept and begged for his favor.
At Bethel God found him,
and there he spoke with us.
5The LORD is the God of Armies;
the LORD is the name by which he is remembered.
6But you, with your God’s help, must return.
Hold on to loyal love and justice,
and wait for your God continually.
7A merchant with dishonest scales in his hand loves to cheat.
8Ephraim says, “I have become rich indeed;
I have gained wealth for myself.
In all my hard work
no one will find any wrongdoing that counts as sin.”
9But I have been the LORD your God since you were in the land of Egypt;
I will make you live in tents again, as in the days of the appointed festival.
10I spoke to the prophets;
I gave them vision after vision,
and through the prophets I spoke in parables.
11If Gilead is wicked, they have surely come to nothing.
In Gilgal they sacrifice bulls;
their altars too will be like heaps of stones
along the furrows of a field.
12Jacob fled to the land of Aram;
Israel worked to earn a wife,
and for a wife he tended sheep.
13By a prophet the LORD brought Israel up from Egypt,
and by a prophet Israel was kept safe.
14Ephraim has bitterly provoked God,
so his Lord will leave the guilt of his bloodshed on him
and pay him back for his contempt.
fields.summary: Israel, like Jacob its ancestor, is deceitful, and God will repay them.

fields.title: Hosea 13
fields.body_html:
Ephraim’s idols

1When Ephraim spoke, people trembled;
he was exalted in Israel.
But he became guilty through Baal, and he died.
2Now they sin more and more and have made themselves a cast image from their silver, idols shaped by their own skill,
every one of them the work of craftsmen.
People say of them,
“Human beings who offer sacrifice kiss calves!”
3So they will be like the morning mist,
like the dew that vanishes early,
like chaff swept by a storm from the threshing floor,
like smoke drifting out through a window.
4But I am the LORD your God, and have been since the land of Egypt;
you are to know no god but me,
and there is no savior except me.
5I cared for you in the wilderness,
in a land of burning drought.
6When they had pasture, they ate their fill;
they were full, and their hearts grew proud;
that is why they forgot me.
7So I have become like a lion to them;
like a leopard I will lurk beside the road.
8I will attack them like a bear robbed of her cubs
and tear open their chests;
I will devour them there like a lioness;
wild animals will tear them to pieces.
9You are destroyed, Israel,
because you are against me, your helper.
10Where is your king now,
who could save you in all your cities?
Where are your rulers, of whom you said,
“Give me a king and officials”?
11I give you a king in my anger,
and in my fury I take him away.

12Ephraim’s guilt is wrapped up;
his sin is kept in store.
13The pains of childbirth come upon him,
but he is a child without sense;
when the time comes, he does not move into the opening of the womb.
14Shall I ransom them from the power of Sheol?
Shall I redeem them from death?
O death, where are your plagues? O Sheol, where is your sting?
Compassion is hidden from my eyes.
15Though he thrives among his brothers,
an east wind will come, a wind of the LORD blowing up from the desert;
his spring will fail and his fountain dry up.
An enemy will plunder his storehouse of every treasure.

Samaria’s guilt

16Samaria must bear her guilt,
because she rebelled against her God.
By the sword they will fall;
their little children will be dashed to pieces,
her pregnant women ripped open.
fields.summary: Israel turned to Baal and calf idols and forgot God, and God will be like a lion against them, yet God will ransom them from death.

fields.title: Hosea 14
fields.body_html:
Return to the LORD

1Return, Israel, to the LORD your God,
for your guilt has made you stumble.
2Take words with you
and return to the LORD.
Say to him, “Take away all guilt, and accept what is good,
and we will offer our lips in place of bulls.
3Assyria cannot save us; we will not ride on horses.
Never again will we say ‘Our god’ to what our own hands have made,
for in you the orphan finds compassion.”
4I will heal their unfaithfulness;
I will love them freely,
for my anger has turned away from them.
5To Israel I will be like the dew;
he will blossom like a lily
and send down his roots like the cedars of Lebanon.
6His young shoots will spread out;
his beauty will be like the olive tree’s,
his fragrance like the cedars of Lebanon.
7Those who live in his shade will come back;
they will flourish like grain and blossom like the vine;
his fame will be like the wine of Lebanon.

8Ephraim, what more have I to do with idols?
I am the one who answers him and watches over him. I am like a cypress, green and full of leaves;
your fruit comes from me.
9Who is wise enough to understand these things?
Who is discerning enough to know them?
For the ways of the LORD are right; the righteous walk in them,
but rebels stumble in them.
fields.summary: God calls Israel to return and confess, and promises to heal their unfaithfulness and love them freely. Israel will blossom like a lily.

fields.title: Conclusion
fields.body_html:
Who is wise enough to understand these things? Who is discerning enough to know them? For the ways of the LORD are right; the righteous walk in them, but rebels stumble in them.

— Hosea 14:9

Hosea ends like a book of wisdom, not like a book of prophecy. After fourteen chapters of grief and anger and astonishing tenderness, a last voice steps back and speaks to whoever has read this far. These things must be understood. The ways of the LORD are right, and the same road that the righteous walk in is the one on which the rebels stumble.

The question the book leaves with you

Hosea’s hearers did not doubt that God existed. They went to the shrines, kept the festivals, and cried out, “My God, we, Israel, know you!” What Hosea asked them was whether they knew him at all: whether their love was a covenant or a mood, the steady faithfulness of a marriage or “like the morning mist, like the dew that vanishes early in the day.” It is the question the book leaves with every reader. Not whether we are religious, but whether we know the God who says, “I want loyal love, not sacrifice.”

The book’s answer to that question is not first an instruction but a portrait. Before it tells Israel to return, it shows the God they would be returning to: a husband who goes into the wilderness to win back an unfaithful wife, a father who taught his son to walk, a Holy One whose heart turns over within him rather than let his people go. The call to “Take words with you and return to the LORD” is only possible because he has already said, “I will love them freely.”

Where the story goes next

Hosea’s warnings came true within his lifetime. The second book of Kings tells how Samaria fell to Assyria after a three-year siege and how the people of the northern kingdom were carried away, “because the Israelites had sinned against the LORD their God”. The southern kingdom, Judah, which Hosea warned more than once, would follow it into exile a little over a century later.

But the promises did not fall with Samaria. Paul and Peter heard them being kept in their own day, as people who had never been God’s people were called “children of the living God”. Matthew saw the Son called out of Egypt. Jesus took Hosea’s “mercy, not sacrifice” as a summary of what God had always wanted. And the New Testament takes up Hosea’s great picture and completes it: the church is the bride, and Christ the bridegroom who gave himself for her.

Where to go from here

Hosea has given preachers some of their most searching texts, and several of the best sermons on them are in this library. A few places to begin:

  • On the love that buys back (Hosea 3). Frances Ridley Havergal’s Christ for Us, which takes Hosea 3:3 as Christ’s promise of himself to the soul he redeems; and Charles H. Spurgeon’s reading for February 4 in Morning by Morning, on the LORD’s love for Israel in Hosea 3:1.
  • On wilderness and betrothal (Hosea 2). Spurgeon’s readings for July 18 and July 22 in The Cheque Book of the Bank of Faith, on Hosea 2:14 and 2:19–20.
  • On love that does not last (Hosea 6–7). Robert Murray M’Cheyne’s sermon The Impressions of Natural Men (Hosea 6:4), on the difference between being moved and being changed; and Spurgeon’s reading for June 23 in Morning by Morning, on the loaf not turned (Hosea 7:8).
  • On seeking the LORD (Hosea 10:12). Charles G. Finney’s Breaking Up the Fallow Ground, a practical call to self-examination and confession, and Spurgeon’s reading for April 1 in Evening by Evening.
  • On the ropes of love (Hosea 11). Spurgeon’s reading for May 20 in Evening by Evening, on Hosea 11:4.
  • On coming home (Hosea 14). M’Cheyne’s What Have I to Do Any More with Idols? (Hosea 14:8), preached at the close of a communion Sabbath; Alexander Maclaren’s The Dew and the Plants (Hosea 14:5–6); and Spurgeon’s reading for October 22 in Morning by Morning, on “I will love them freely” (Hosea 14:4).
  • On Hosea and the gospel. Augustine’s The City of God, whose eighteenth book, chapter 28, gathers what Hosea and Amos foretold of Christ and the calling of the nations; and Jerome’s letter to Paulinus (Letter LIII in The Letters of St. Jerome), which sketches the hidden meaning of each of the twelve prophets, beginning with Hosea.

You can also go the other way, from the text to the classics. Every reference to Hosea in this library can be tapped to read the verse, and the Scripture pages gather, chapter by chapter, what the great writers of the church have said about each passage of this book.

And then read Hosea again, beginning with the eleventh chapter. Once you have heard God remember his people’s childhood, the hard chapters around it read differently. They are the anger of a love that will not stop loving:

I led them with human cords, with ropes of love. To them I was like someone who lifts the yoke off their jaws, and I bent down to them and fed them.

— Hosea 11:4
